# DESIGNING FOR EVERYONE WITHOUT DESIGNING FOR NO ONE
## Cultural inclusion, accessibility, internationalisation and safety in a global digital product

**Product, Design & Policy standard | v2.0**
**Author:** [Head of Product Design] · **Contributors:** Platform Engineering, Content Ops, Trust & Safety, Legal, Accessibility
**Issued:** [date] · **Next scheduled review:** +6 months, and on any new-market launch, any new AI-generated surface, or any Sev-1 cultural incident (§10.4)
**Companion artefacts:** Annex A string glossary and do-not-translate list · Annex B locale tier matrix · Annex C review checklists (content, visual, a11y, safety) · Annex D named owner register and RACI · Annex E bidi/pseudo-loc test corpus. None is required to read this document.

---

## FRONT MATTER — the one page for people who will not read §2

**Five workstreams, not one project.** Internationalisation (engineering), Localisation (content ops), Accessibility (design systems + QA + legal), Cultural inclusion & safety (policy), and Regulatory & payments localisation (legal + platform). Different owners, different clock speeds, different failure modes, different budget lines. §1.

**The sequencing rule.** *Architecture first, content second, judgement always.* Anything that is structurally expensive to retrofit — Unicode handling, RTL, data models, accessibility semantics, locale plumbing — is **P0 and blocks first launch**. Anything that is content or policy is revisited continuously and never "done". §11 is the P0 gate; nothing ships to a first non-source locale until every P0 row is green.

**The honest limit.** Most inadvertent offence is *avoidable by process* — this document is largely that process. A small residue is **not** avoidable, because some user groups' values are mutually exclusive and some jurisdictions' law is hostile to some of our users. §9 is the framework for that residue, including what is non-negotiable and who signs. We do not pretend the residue away, and we do not use its existence to excuse the avoidable 90%.

**What we are asking for.** Adoption of the P0 gate (§11), the named-owner register (Annex D), the minimum safety floor (§9.2), the accessibility conformance target of **WCAG 2.2 AA** (§5.1), and the research budget in §8.4 — because every **[R]** item in this document is a research task we have not yet done, and shipping them as if they were findings is the single most likely way this fails.

---

## §0 Scope, evidence tags, and the rules of this document

### 0.1 How to read the claims

| Tag | Type | Example | How settled |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable / standardised** | WCAG success criteria, Unicode/CLDR data, BCP 47, ICU plural categories, statutory deadlines | Should be *certain*. Cite the standard or the statute; never estimate |
| **[L]** | **Legal, jurisdiction-specific** | Data residency, age gating, content law, accessibility statutes, sensitive-attribute law | Verifiable **but only by counsel, per jurisdiction**. Never settled by a product manager reading a blog post |
| **[R]** | **Researchable** | Whether users in market X parse a hamburger menu; device/network mix; which gesture reads as rude; expansion behaviour of our actual strings | Requires in-market research (§8). Do not infer from diaspora users, from your own team, or from a rule of thumb |
| **[D]** | **Design decision** | Locale tiering, which markets get full localisation, default privacy posture, cost estimates | A choice with a cost, owned by a named person in Annex D |

Tags are applied comprehensively from §2 onward, not decoratively. Where a statement is untagged it is an argument, not a claim of fact. **The most common failure in this discipline is an [R] claim written down as [V]** — v1.0 of this document committed that failure three times; the corrections are in §12.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out of scope |
|---|---|
| Product architecture, UI, content, identity/data model, visual semantics, AI behaviour, moderation policy, device/network inclusion, governance | Market-entry sequencing, commercial sizing, pricing strategy |
| Accessibility as a global equity issue *and* a legal obligation | Marketing campaign creative (governed by §3–§4, owned by Brand) |
| Regulatory localisation *as it lands in product surfaces* (consent UI, age gates, data residency, payment methods) | The corporate compliance programme itself |
| Named value tensions and the framework for resolving them (§9) | Legal advice. Every **[L]** item requires counsel in each jurisdiction before ship |

### 0.3 The two rules

**Rule 1 — every requirement carries an owner and a cost.** Owners in this document are given as *role + Annex D reference*; Annex D carries the individual name and is maintained as a live document, because names change and a stale name is worse than none. Costs are order-of-magnitude engineering estimates **[D]**, given so that a requirement can be traded off honestly rather than silently dropped at the first schedule crunch. A row with a blank cost has not been thought through and should be challenged in review.

**Rule 2 — architecture first, content second, judgement always.** Retrofit cost is the reason. Public estimates for i18n retrofit versus greenfield cluster around 3–10× and accessibility remediation similarly, but these are **[R]** industry rules of thumb, not measured facts about our codebase; the defensible version of the claim is structural — an interface built on `margin-left`, string concatenation and a `first_name`/`last_name` schema cannot be fixed by a translator, a designer or a policy, only by a rewrite. Content and policy decisions, by contrast, are cheap to revise and should be revised continuously. This is an argument for sequencing (§11), not for perfectionism.

---

## §1 The five workstreams, separated

| Workstream | Question it answers | Owner (Annex D) | Clock speed | Failure mode if fused with the others |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Internationalisation (i18n)** | Can the system *hold* any language, script, name, date, currency, address? | Platform Engineering — D-01 | Once, deeply, up front | Gets deprioritised as "translation work" and becomes un-fixable architectural debt |
| **Localisation (l10n)** | Is the content correct, natural, and legally adequate in this locale? | Content Ops + regional leads — D-02 | Continuous | Becomes a bulk-translation cost line; quality invisible until support tickets spike |
| **Accessibility (a11y)** | Can disabled users complete every task independently? | Design Systems + QA, with Legal — D-03 | Continuous, with hard statutory dates | Treated as an edge case rather than a legal obligation and a ~16% / 1.3bn population **[V]** (WHO, *Global report on health equity for persons with disabilities*, 2022) |
| **Cultural inclusion & safety** | Does this respect, endanger, erase or misrepresent anyone? | Trust & Safety / Policy, exec-accountable — D-04 | Continuous, with incident-driven spikes | Reduced to a checklist; no one is empowered to say "we are not shipping this" |
| **Regulatory & payments localisation** | Is the product lawful, payable and identity-appropriate in this market? | Legal + Platform + Payments — D-05 | Per-market, gated | Assumed to be "market entry, not product", so consent UI, age gates, data residency and local payment rails arrive as launch-blocking surprises |

The fifth workstream is added in this version deliberately. Data residency, age assurance, consent regimes, content law, e-invoicing, local payment methods and identity verification are **product features with UI, data models and failure states**, not commercial questions. Declaring "market-entry sequencing" out of scope does not dispose of them.

**Corollary — translation is the last 10% of localisation.** If the string is `"You have " + count + " new message" + (count==1?"":"s")`, no translator can save it. The architecture decides the ceiling on quality; the content pipeline only decides whether you reach it.

---

## §2 Foundation: internationalisation architecture (P0)

Cost estimates are engineering-weeks for a product of our current surface area **[D]**, and are for *building in*, not retrofitting.

### 2.1 Text, encoding and typography

| # | Requirement | Detail | Tag | Owner | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1.1 | **Encoding** | UTF-8 end-to-end: storage, transport, DB and collation, logs, filenames, exports. Support the full plane range including emoji and rare CJK (`utf8mb4`, not `utf8`) | **[V]** | D-01 | 2w |
| 2.1.2 | **Normalisation — carefully** | Normalise to **NFC for display and for comparison keys**, and preserve the user's original bytes for display. Do **not** apply NFKC to human-entered identifiers (it collapses distinct characters). Do **not** ad-hoc normalise passwords: use a documented profile (PRECIS `OpaqueString`, RFC 8265) applied *identically* at set and at verify. Destructive normalisation on input is a login-failure bug generator | **[V]** | D-01 | 1w |
| 2.1.3 | **Locale identity** | BCP 47 tags throughout (`pt-BR`, `zh-Hant-HK`, `sr-Latn-RS`, `es-419`). Never two-letter country codes as language proxies; never a flag as a language identifier (§4.3) | **[V]** | D-01 | 1w |
| 2.1.4 | **Decouple the axes** | UI language, regional formats, currency, timezone, **content region** and **legal/data region** are **six independent settings**, user-changeable, persisted per account. A Japanese speaker in Germany paying in euros under EU law is normal. Anti-pattern: inferring language from IP and locking it; IP may *suggest* a default, never impose one | **[D]** | D-01 | 3w |
| 2.1.5 | **Text expansion** | Expansion is length-banded, not a flat percentage. Working budget from IBM/Microsoft guidance: source strings ≤10 chars may expand **200–300%**; 11–20 chars ~180%; 21–30 ~160%; 31–50 ~140%; 50+ ~130%. CJK typically contracts. **These are planning heuristics, not standards** — measure against our own string corpus in pseudo-loc. No fixed-width containers, no truncation-by-design, no text baked into images | **[R]** | D-01 + D-02 | 3w (design system) |
| 2.1.6 | **Fonts** | Script coverage for Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari and other Indic, Thai, Lao, Khmer, Myanmar, CJK (with correct regional glyph variants — do not render Japanese with a Simplified Chinese font), Hangul, Ethiopic. Increased line-height for stacked marks (Thai, Devanagari, Vietnamese). Subset, lazy-load and per-script split to protect payload (§7) | **[V]** | D-01 | 3w |
| 2.1.7 | **Pluralisation** | ICU MessageFormat with all six CLDR categories (`zero/one/two/few/many/other`). **Arabic uses all six; Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Thai and Vietnamese use only `other`.** Never `if (n==1)` | **[V]** | D-01 | 2w |
| 2.1.8 | **Gender, case and ordinals** | ICU `select` for grammatical gender; ICU `selectordinal`. Never interpolate names or nouns into case-inflected sentences (Slavic, Finnish, Hungarian). Prefer restructuring ("Owner: {name}") over grammatical gymnastics | **[V]** | D-02 | 1w |
| 2.1.9 | **No concatenation. Ever.** | One string = one complete, ordered sentence with **named** placeholders (`{count}`, not `%s`), plus a mandatory `description` and a screenshot/context link visible to the translator | **[V]** | D-01 | 2w |
| 2.1.10 | **Collation, search, sort** | ICU collation per locale (German phonebook vs dictionary order differ); diacritic- and case-insensitive matching; CJK and Thai word segmentation; Arabic alef/hamza/tatweel normalisation; transliteration search (`tokyo` → 東京, `moskva` → Москва) | **[V]** | D-01 | 4w |
| 2.1.11 | **Input methods** | Full IME support. Suppress validation, autocomplete-submit and shortcut handling during composition using `compositionstart`/`compositionend` and `event.isComposing` — not `keyup` heuristics. No Latin-only regex on any user-entered field, ever | **[V]** | D-01 | 2w |
| 2.1.12 | **Units and formats** | Locale-driven measurement systems (metric/imperial), paper size (A4/Letter) in any print or PDF output, clothing/shoe sizing tables where relevant, 12h/24h clock, decimal and grouping separators (`1.234,56`), and negative/currency placement — all from CLDR, never hard-coded | **[V]** | D-01 | 2w |
| 2.1.13 | **Pseudo-localisation in CI** | `[!!! Ŧḗẋŧ ḗẋƥȧƞsīǿƞ !!!]` build, blocking merge on overflow, clipping, and hard-coded strings. Paired with a **hard-coded-string linter** (`eslint-plugin-i18next` / equivalent, `no-literal-string`) and an **RTL snapshot test** (§2.2) in the same gate | **[D]** | D-01 | 2w + 0.5w/quarter upkeep |

### 2.2 Bidirectional (RTL) support — P0, not a later project

Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, Pashto, Dhivehi. Owner **D-01/D-03**, cost ~4w in the design system if done first, an order of magnitude more later.

- **Logical CSS properties throughout** (`margin-inline-start`, `padding-block`, `text-align: start`, `inset-inline-end`) from the first component. Physical directions are banned in the design system lint rules. **[V]**
- **Mirroring rule.** Mirror icons that depict **direction or progression** — back/forward arrows, undo/redo, progress bars, sliders, indentation, list bullets, speech-bubble tails, **and pointing hands or directional gesture glyphs**. Do **not** mirror icons depicting **physical objects with a fixed form or culturally fixed orientation** — clocks and analogue timers, checkmarks, musical notation, physical media, logos and wordmarks. (Corrects the v1.0 error, which excluded gestures from mirroring and would produce backwards affordances in Arabic and Hebrew.) **[V]** — Material Design and Apple HIG bidirectionality guidance.
- **Bidi isolation on every interpolated value.** Wrap names, numbers, prices, URLs, file names and user content in isolates (`\u2066…\u2069` / `<bdi>` / CSS `unicode-bidi: isolate`). Un-isolated interpolation is *the* source of mangled phone numbers and reversed prices. **[V]**
- **Swipe and animation semantics invert.** "Next" is right-to-left. Test carousels, back-swipe, onboarding progress, chart axes and timeline direction. **[R]** for anything gesture-based.
- **Test corpus (Annex E), mandatory in CI:** pure Arabic; pure Hebrew; **mixed-direction strings** (Arabic sentence + Latin brand name + Western digits + currency symbol + URL); Arabic with Eastern Arabic-Indic digits; Hebrew with parentheses and quotation marks; RTL name in an LTR U

# WHERE WE GROW NEXT
## International expansion: demand entry and supply entry as two separate decisions

**Board decision paper | v2.0**
*(The management committee counterpart, with vendor-level detail and the full research brief, is Annex 1 and is not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track structure, the beachhead selection method and its result, the positioning boundary, the channel sequence, the origin rule in §6.2, and **€290k (plus €45k contingency) to fund Gate 0**. Country choice becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions, not one. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners; fusing them into a single geography is how mid-sized brands lose margin in both. We propose a **Demand Track** entering **Japan** as beachhead — chosen on the scored criteria in §3.2, not asserted — with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin while retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment and **India as a source of certified organic fibre and yarn only**. The two tracks meet at one technical point and it is not the one an earlier draft claimed: preference eligibility is governed by **rules of origin, not by where the sewing happens**, which produces a single hard rule — **fibre and yarn may cross borders; fabric may not** (§6.2). Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics"; Uniqlo and Muji own that ground in Japan permanently and will out-execute us on it forever. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair — at a price architecture that never competes with either (§4). Channels are sequenced credibility-first and capital-last: distributor and wholesale before any entity, lease or local payroll, so that a failed entry costs a contract rather than a balance sheet (§5, §10.3). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that Vietnamese vertical certified-organic fabric capacity exists at our quality and volume, and that Japan out-scores Korea on willingness-to-pay for provenance. Gate 0 exists to test exactly those two things, and §3.6 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to the core

### 0.1 How to read the figures

Three kinds of number appear here, tagged on first use. Confusing them is the main way strategy papers mislead their own authors.

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, rule of origin, labelling statute, tax threshold | Should be *certain* — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, by counsel and a customs broker |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Import volumes, competitor retail prices, wholesale margin norms, CAC | Trade and customs data: ±[15]%. **Niche premium segment sizing: ±[40]% at best** | Gate 0, by field research |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, channel mix, vendor count, price points | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this Board |

Everything touching tariff preference, rules of origin, labelling or entity law is **[V]** — a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact in this paper. Preference regimes phase down, graduate and expire; §6.5 prices that risk rather than merely noting it.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered through one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiating existing Portuguese/Turkish terms |
| Substantiation infrastructure (required by EU law regardless) | M&A, licensing, franchising |
| The organisational capacity to run both without degrading the core | Category extension beyond market-fit adaptation |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every commitment to the new market carries a stated cost to the core business** — attention, working capital, or inventory risk. This is not a slogan; it is enforced numerically in §2.4 (attention budget) and §8.3 (working-capital draw). A line item in this paper without a named cost to the core has not been thought through.

Baseline, to be confirmed at Gate 0: revenue €[78]m **[R]**, gross margin [58]%, EBITDA [8.5]%, [210] FTE, [62]% of revenue in DE/NL/Nordics, wholesale/DTC split [55/45].

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, lead-time inventory, defect rate and audit overhead** — and does the preference actually apply to *our* bill of materials? |

**Corollary 1 — cheap labour is not cheap.** FOB price is the smallest and least reliable term in landed cost. A [15]% FOB saving **[D]** is erased by an [11.5]% MFN duty if origin fails **[V]**, by a [4]-week lead-time extension financed as inventory, by a [2]-point defect rate, or by one labour finding that costs a retail listing. Sourcing decisions are landed-cost-after-risk decisions.

# DESIGNING FOR EVERYONE WITHOUT DESIGNING FOR NO ONE
## Cultural inclusion, accessibility and localisation in a global digital product

**Product & design guidance | v1.0**
*Companion artefacts — the string glossary, locale tier matrix, review checklists and vendor brief — are Annexes A–D and are not required to read this document.*

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

"Make the product inclusive globally" is not one workstream; it is **four**, and conflating them is the standard way this fails. **Internationalisation (i18n)** is an engineering property of the codebase. **Localisation (l10n)** is a content and operations pipeline. **Accessibility (a11y)** is a conformance and quality discipline with legal force. **Cultural inclusion and safety** is a policy and governance function that makes judgement calls no checklist can make. They have different owners, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different budget lines. Treating them as one "global readiness" ticket produces a product that is technically translatable and culturally tone-deaf, or culturally sensitive and unusable on a 2GB Android phone. The load-bearing rule of this document is **§0.3: architecture first, content second, judgement always** — i18n and a11y must be built into the foundation because retrofitting them costs a documented multiple of building them in; cultural content decisions can and should be revisited continuously. Finally, this document refuses one premise in the brief: a global product **cannot** avoid offending every user group, because some user groups' values are mutually exclusive and some are encoded in law that conflicts with user safety. §8 states the decision framework we use when that happens, rather than pretending it does not.

### 0.1 How to read the claims

| Tag | Type | Example | How settled |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable / standardised** | WCAG success criteria, Unicode CLDR data, BCP 47 tags, ICU plural categories, statutory deadlines | Should be *certain*. Cite the standard; never estimate |
| **[R]** | **Researchable** | Whether users in market X understand a hamburger menu; device/network mix; which gesture reads as rude | Requires in-market research. Do not infer from diaspora users or from your own team |
| **[D]** | **Design decision** | Locale tiering, which markets get full localisation, default privacy posture | A choice with a cost, owned by a named person |

Anything tagged **[R]** in this document is a research task, not a finding. The single most common failure in cultural design is a **[R]** claim written down as **[V]**.

| In scope | Out of scope |
|---|---|
| Product architecture, UI, content, identity model, AI behaviour, moderation policy, governance | Market-entry sequencing and commercial sizing |
| Accessibility as a global equity issue, not only a compliance item | Marketing campaign creative (governed by the same content rules, different owner) |
| Named tensions and the framework for resolving them | Legal advice — every **[V]** legal item requires counsel per jurisdiction |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every recommendation names its owner and its cost.** A guideline without an owner is a wish; a guideline without a cost has not been costed and will be dropped at the first schedule crunch. And: **inclusion decisions that are cheap now are expensive later at a documented multiple** — industry experience puts i18n retrofit at roughly 3–10× greenfield cost **[R]**, and accessibility remediation post-launch similarly. This is the argument for sequencing, not for perfectionism.

## §1 The four workstreams, separated

|---|---|---|---|
| **Internationalisation** | Can the system *hold* any language, script, name, date, currency, address? | Engineering (platform) | Gets deprioritised as "translation work" and becomes an un-fixable architectural debt |

These are engineering requirements, mostly **[V]** against published standards. They belong in the definition of done before the first market launch, ideally before the first line of production code.

| Requirement | Detail |

| Encoding | UTF-8 end-to-end (storage, transport, DB collation, logs, filenames). Normalise to Unicode NFC on input **[V]** |
| Locale identity | BCP 47 tags (`pt-BR`, `zh-Hant-HK`, `sr-Latn-RS`), never two-letter country codes as language proxies **[V]** |
| Decouple the axes | UI language, regional formats, currency, timezone and content region are **five separate user settings**. A Japanese speaker in Germany paying in euros is normal |

| Pluralisation | ICU MessageFormat with all six CLDR plural categories (`zero/one/two/few/many/other`). Arabic uses all six; Japanese uses one **[V]** |
| Grammatical gender & case | ICU `select` for gender; never interpolate names into case-inflected sentences (Slavic, Finnish). Prefer sentence restructuring over grammatical gymnastics |
| No concatenation | Ever. One string = one complete, ordered, translator-visible sentence with named placeholders |
| Collation & search | ICU collation for sorting; diacritic- and case-insensitive search; CJK word segmentation; Arabic alef/hamza normalisation; transliteration search (`tokyo` → 東京) |

Not a skin. Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu.

- Use **logical CSS properties** (`margin-inline-start`, not `margin-left`) throughout the design system from day one.
- Mirror **directional** icons (back arrows, progress, undo, list bullets, sliders); do **not** mirror physical-object icons (clocks, checkmarks, physical media, logos, most gestures) **[V]**.

- Swipe semantics invert: "swipe forward" is right-to-left. Test carousels, back-swipe, and progress animation.
- RTL must be in the **first** release of the design system, not a later "RTL project". Retrofit is the expensive path.

### 2.3 Data models that don't exclude people

| Field | Wrong assumption | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Names** | first + last, Latin only, 2–30 chars | Single required `full name` (Unicode, ≥100 chars, apostrophes/hyphens/spaces valid) plus optional `display name`. Support mononyms (Indonesian), multiple surnames (Spanish, Portuguese), patronymics (Icelandic, Russian), particles (van, de, bin), family-name-first display (CJK, Hungarian), and optional phonetic fields (furigana) where the market requires them |
| **Addresses** | street / city / state / ZIP, all required | Locale-driven field sets and ordering (Google's address metadata / libaddressinput). Japan has no street names; Ireland had no postcodes until recently; many countries have no "state". Never require a field a country doesn't have |
| **Phone** | 10 digits, US format | E.164 storage, libphonenumber validation, country selector defaulting to detected region but freely changeable |
| **Dates** | MM/DD/YYYY, Gregorian only, week starts Sunday | ISO 8601 in storage; CLDR-driven display; support Gregorian,

### 2.2 Bidirectional (RTL) support

Not a skin. Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu.

- Use **logical CSS properties** (`margin-inline-start`, not `margin-left`) throughout the design system from day one.
- Mirror **directional** icons (back arrows, progress, undo, list bullets, sliders); do **not** mirror physical-object icons (clocks, checkmarks, physical media, logos, most gestures) **[V]**.
- Numbers and Latin substrings remain LTR inside RTL text — use Unicode bidi isolation (`\u2068…\u2069`) around interpolated values to prevent mangled phone numbers and prices.
- Swipe semantics invert: "swipe forward" is right-to-left. Test carousels, back-swipe, and progress animation.
- RTL must be in the **first** release of the design system, not a later "RTL project". Retrofit is the expensive path.

### 2.3 Data models that don't exclude people

| Field | Wrong assumption | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Names** | first + last, Latin only, 2–30 chars | Single required `full name` (Unicode, ≥100 chars, apostrophes/hyphens/spaces valid) plus optional `display name`. Support mononyms (Indonesian), multiple surnames (Spanish, Portuguese), patronymics (Icelandic, Russian), particles (van, de, bin), family-name-first display (CJK, Hungarian), and optional phonetic fields (furigana) where the market requires them |

| **Phone** | 10 digits, US format | E.164 storage, libphonenumber validation, country selector defaulting to detected region but freely changeable |
| **Dates** | MM/DD/YYYY, Gregorian only, week starts Sunday | ISO 8601 in storage; CLDR-driven display; support Gregorian,

# Critique: "Designing for Everyone Without Designing for No One" (v1.0)

## 1. Blocking issues

**1.1 The document is truncated mid-sentence.** It ends at `support Gregorian,` inside the §2.3 dates row. This is not a stylistic complaint: the paper forward-references sections that do not exist — §8 ("the decision framework we use when [values conflict]"), the governance function in §1, the "sequencing" argument in §0.3, Annexes A–D. The single most provocative claim in the paper (that the brief's premise is impossible) is deliberately deferred to §8, and §8 never arrives. The reader is left with the refusal and none of the resolution. As delivered, this is a fragment, not a deliverable.

**1.2 Two of the three things the user asked for are missing.** The request was "features, design considerations, and **content guidelines**." What exists is i18n engineering architecture (§2.1–2.3) — roughly 15% of the surface area of the brief — plus a framing section. There is nothing on:

- imagery, photography and representation; avatar/skin-tone/hair systems
- colour, number and symbol semantics (white/mourning, 4 in CJK, red, owls, pigs, thumbs-up, OK gesture, hand-shape emoji)
- iconography that doesn't travel (mailbox, trash can, piggy bank, church/graduation-cap metaphors)
- **flags as language selectors** — the canonical anti-pattern, and it is missing from a document that otherwise dwells on BCP 47
- formality registers and honorifics (T–V distinction, Japanese keigo, Korean speech levels), plain-language and reading-level rules, idiom/humour/sports metaphor/pun bans in source copy
- calendars, holidays, weekends (Fri–Sat vs Sat–Sun), Ramadan/fasting modes, prayer-time and religious observance
- gender and pronoun options; sensitive attributes (caste, ethnicity, sexuality, religion) and the specific danger of collecting them in jurisdictions that criminalise the group
- maps, disputed borders, place names, currency/flag of contested territories — a routine cause of bans and offence
- moderation and safety across languages (classifier coverage gaps in low-resource languages, native-speaker reviewers, appeals)
- AI/LLM behaviour: bias in generation, refusal behaviour, cultural defaults, evaluation sets per locale — flagged as in-scope in §0.2 and then never addressed
- device, network and cost inclusion — the "2GB Android phone" is invoked rhetorically in the opening paragraph and never returned to
- research method (how to actually produce the **[R]** findings), in-market testing, cultural review/red-team process, incident escalation, metrics, launch gates, owner list

**1.3 Accessibility is asserted as one of the four pillars and then not specified.** A11y appears in one table row. No conformance target (WCAG 2.2 AA), no legal instruments (EN 301 549, European Accessibility Act deadline, ADA/Section 508, AODA), no assistive-technology test matrix, nothing on captions/transcripts/sign, contrast, target size, motion sensitivity, cognitive accessibility, or dynamic type. The paper's own §0.3 claims a documented cost multiple for post-launch remediation without a source. For a brief that named accessibility explicitly, this is under-served.

## 2. Technical accuracy errors — and they land on **[V]**-tagged claims

The document declares that "the single most common failure in cultural design is a **[R]** claim written down as **[V]**," then commits that failure at least three times:

- **Text expansion of 30–50% / CJK contraction 40–60% is tagged [V].** These are widely repeated rules of thumb, not standardised values; actual expansion depends on string length (short UI labels can expand 200–300%). Either cite a source or re-tag **[R]** and replace with the length-banded IBM/Microsoft guidance.
- **"Japanese uses one" plural category is wrong.** CLDR assigns Japanese only `other`. Arabic using all six is correct. This is a factual error inside a **[V]** row about the exact standard being cited.
- **"do not mirror … most gestures" is tagged [V] and is contrary to standard guidance.** Material and Apple guidance is that icons depicting *direction*, including pointing hands and directional gestures, should mirror; only physical objects and culturally fixed forms should not. As written it will produce backwards affordances in Arabic and Hebrew.

Further accuracy notes:

- **"Japan has no street names"** is an overstatement. Japan uses a prefecture/city/ward/block/lot system; some thoroughfares are named. Say "most Japanese addresses are not street-based" and the point survives scrutiny.
- **"Normalise to Unicode NFC on input"** needs a carve-out: do not destructively normalise passwords or cryptographic inputs, and be explicit about NFC vs NFKC for identifiers vs display. As stated it is an invitation to a login-failure bug.
- **"15%+ population [R]"** is closer to **[V]** — WHO puts disability at ~16% / 1.3bn. Citable, not researchable.
- **Name field cap "≥100 chars"** — pick a generous ceiling (255) and, more importantly, state "no character-class validation," which is the actual failure mode.
- **IME guidance** should name the mechanism (`compositionstart`/`compositionend`, `event.isComposing`) rather than "not bound to `keyup`," which is a symptom.

## 3. The document violates its own two rules

- **§0.3: "Every recommendation names its owner and its cost."** Not one of the ~20 requirements in §2.1, nor any in §2.2 or §2.3, carries an owner or a cost. §1 gives *functions* ("Engineering (platform)"), not named owners, which the rule explicitly rejects ("a guideline without an owner is a wish"). Either add owner and cost columns to §2 tables, or soften the rule to "every workstream," or drop it. As it stands the rule is decorative — the same failure the source document (§0.3 of the board paper) was written to prevent.
- **§0.3: "architecture first, content second, judgement always."** Declared to be the load-bearing rule, then never operationalised — there is no sequencing artefact, no P0/P1/P2 tiering, no "definition of done before first market launch" list, no gate. The claim that this is "the argument for sequencing" is left as an assertion.

Related: the tag taxonomy is inherited wholesale from the previous artefact but earns its keep less well here. In the board paper the tags disciplined spend decisions. Here, a large majority of statements are untagged, so the tags read as house-style ornament rather than as a working device. Either tag comprehensively in §2 onward or reduce the apparatus to a short note.

## 4. Framing and argument

**4.1 The four-workstream separation is the strongest thing in the paper** and should be preserved verbatim. So should the corollary that "translation is the last 10% of localisation" with the concatenation example — it is concrete, memorable and correct.

**4.2 The refusal of the brief's premise is well-judged but imprecise, and currently unpaid-for.** The user asked not to "inadvertently exclude or offend." The paper answers a different, harder question: how to handle *deliberate* value conflicts. Those are distinct. Most inadvertent offence *is* avoidable by process; only a residue involves mutually exclusive values or hostile law. The paper should say so — otherwise the refusal reads as a rhetorical move that lowers the bar on the avoidable 90%. And having raised the conflict, it must actually deliver the framework (harm asymmetry, who bears the risk, minimum-safety floor vs local adaptation, what is non-negotiable, who signs).

**4.3 Missing fifth workstream, or an explicit statement of why not.** Legal/regulatory localisation (data residency, age gating, consent regimes, content law, e-invoicing) and payment/identity localisation are product features, not market-entry commercial questions, so "market-entry sequencing" being out of scope does not dispose of them. Name where they live.

**4.4 §0.2 out-of-scope on legal advice is right, but §2 is full of statutory adjacency** (labelling, accessibility law, name/ID handling). Add a one-line "counsel per jurisdiction" gate to the relevant rows rather than only in the scope table.

**4.5 Audience mismatch risk.** The register is dense and engineering-facing; the brief implies a cross-functional audience including content, policy and leadership. Consider a one-page front matter with the four workstreams, the P0 list, and the named owners — then let §2 be as dense as it likes.

## 5. Smaller fixes

- Add author, date and review cadence; "v1.0" alone is insufficient for a governance document that claims continuous revisitation of cultural content.
- §2.1 "Decouple the axes" is excellent; add **content region / legal region** as distinct from currency, and note the anti-pattern of inferring language from IP.
- Add: mandatory phone number as an exclusion mechanism (shared devices, gendered phone access in some markets), and mandatory government ID / real-name policies as a safety risk for some users.
- Add: units, paper sizes, sizing systems, address-format-driven shipping validation.
- §2.2 should include a bidi test corpus and a *mixed-direction* string test (Arabic + Latin brand name + number + price), which is where isolation bugs actually appear.
- Pseudo-localisation is well specified; extend the CI gate to include an RTL snapshot test and a hard-coded-string linter, both named.

## 6. What must change before this passes

1. Finish the document — at minimum §3 content guidelines, §4 cultural/visual semantics, §5 accessibility specification, §6 AI and moderation, §7 research method, §8 conflict framework, §9 governance/escalation/metrics, plus a P0 launch gate.
2. Correct the three mis-tagged/incorrect **[V]** claims (expansion figures, Japanese plurals, gesture mirroring) and the Japan address overstatement.
3. Comply with §0.3 — owner and cost columns, or amend the rule.
4. Reconcile the names guidance with the locale-driven principle applied to addresses.
5. Specify the accessibility conformance target and legal instruments.
6. Distinguish avoidable inadvertent offence from irreducible value conflict, and deliver the framework promised for the latter.

**The honest limit.** Most inadvertent offence is *avoidable by process* — this document is largely that process. A small residue is **not** avoidable, because some user groups' values are mutually exclusive and some jurisdictions' law is hostile to some of our users. §9 is the framework for that residue, including what is non-negotiable and who signs. We do not pretend the residue away, and we do not use its existence to excuse the avoidable 90%.

**What we are asking for.** Adoption of the P0 gate (§11), the named-owner register (Annex D), the minimum safety floor (§9.2), the accessibility conformance target of **WCAG 2.2 AA** (§5.1), and the research budget in §8.4 — because every **[R]** item in this document is a research task we have not yet done, and shipping them as if they were findings is the single most likely way this fails.

| **[D]** | **Design decision** | Locale tiering, which markets get full localisation, default privacy posture, cost estimates | A choice with a cost, owned by a named person in Annex D |

Where a statement is untagged it is an argument, not a claim of fact. **The most common failure in this discipline is an [R] claim written down as [V]** — v1.0 of this document committed that failure three times; the corrections are in §12.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

### 0.3 The two rules

**Rule 1 — every requirement carries an owner and a cost.** Owners in this document are given as *role + Annex D reference*; Annex D carries the individual name and is maintained as a live document, because names change and a stale name is worse than none. Costs are order-of-magnitude engineering estimates **[D]**, given so that a requirement can be traded off honestly rather than silently dropped at the first schedule crunch. A row with a blank cost has not been thought through and should be challenged in review.

**Rule 2 — architecture first, content second, judgement always.** Retrofit cost is the reason. Public estimates for i18n retrofit versus greenfield cluster around 3–10× and accessibility remediation similarly, but these are **[R]** industry rules of thumb, not measured facts about our codebase; the defensible version of the claim is structural — an interface built on `margin-left`, string concatenation and a `first_name`/`last_name` schema cannot be fixed by a translator, a designer or a policy, only by a rewrite. Content and policy decisions, by contrast, are cheap to revise and should be revised continuously. This is an argument for sequencing (§11), not for perfectionism.

## §1 The five workstreams, separated

| Workstream | Question it answers | Owner (Annex D) | Clock speed | Failure mode if fused with the others |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Internationalisation (i18n)** | Can the system *hold* any language, script, name, date, currency, address? | Platform Engineering — D-01 | Once, deeply, up front | Gets deprioritised as "translation work" and becomes un-fixable architectural debt |
| **Localisation (l10n)** | Is the content correct, natural, and legally adequate in this locale? | Content Ops + regional leads — D-02 | Continuous | Becomes a bulk-translation cost line; quality invisible until support tickets spike |
| **Accessibility (a11y)** | Can disabled users complete every task independently? | Design Systems + QA, with Legal — D-03 | Continuous, with hard statutory dates | Treated as an edge case rather than a legal obligation and a ~16% / 1.3bn population **[V]** (WHO, *Global report on health equity for persons with disabilities*, 2022) |
| **Cultural inclusion & safety** | Does this respect, endanger, erase or misrepresent anyone? | Trust & Safety / Policy, exec-accountable — D-04 | Continuous, with incident-driven spikes | Reduced to a checklist; no one is empowered to say "we are not shipping this" |
| **Regulatory & payments localisation** | Is the product lawful, payable and identity-appropriate in this market? | Legal + Platform + Payments — D-05 | Per-market, gated | Assumed to be "market entry, not product", so consent UI, age gates, data residency and local payment rails arrive as launch-blocking surprises |

The fifth workstream is added in this version deliberately. Data residency, age assurance, consent regimes, content law, e-invoicing, local payment methods and identity verification are **product features with UI, data models and failure states**, not commercial questions. Declaring "market-entry sequencing" out of scope does not dispose of them.

**Corollary — translation is the last 10% of localisation.** If the string is `"You have " + count + " new message" + (count==1?"":"s")`, no translator can save it. The architecture decides the ceiling on quality; the content pipeline only decides whether you reach it.
